1.title: The Hangar Door
1.subject: An open hangar door at early morning, pale light falling across a swept concrete floor. On the inner wall a large dark screen hangs beside an older whiteboard covered in smudged, unreadable marks. Beyond the apron a railway siding runs past with a line of plain freight wagons. One figure stands in the doorway holding a folded letter, back turned to the viewer.

2.title: The Winter Canteen
2.subject: A plain base canteen in winter, steam on tall windows and grey snow light outside. An old radio sits silent on a shelf. A long table holds cups, an unopened jar and a folded coat. At its far end one person sits facing away with both hands around a cup, while another stands nearby, partly turned, as if deciding whether to sit.

3.title: The Workshop Bench
3.subject: A long railway workshop bench under high industrial windows in late afternoon light. One deep drawer stands open, packed with folders of handwritten sheets. On the bench lie practice joints, small clamps and a worn green marker with its cap off. Apprentices' coats hang by the door, and two figures stand at the bench with their faces turned away.

chapters.title: Green or Red, and Nothing Else

texts.trusted: The new readiness board arrived in a crate larger than the parts it was meant to describe. Mounted beside the old whiteboard, it showed each aircraft as a green or red square and nothing else. Pavel Kresin, who taught young pilots now, called it the most honest thing he had ever seen: no handwriting to argue over. Milan Sarek liked that it matched requests to machines in seconds. Vera Dolin, retired and present because nobody had dared install it without her, asked where the note went. The engineer said notes could be attached. Vera asked who would open them. Nadia Orlov had been asked to write the material for the operations staff who would read the screen, and hers was the last signature the installation needed.
texts.compromised: The new readiness board showed each aircraft as a green or red square, with any qualification stored a layer beneath, where only a patient reader would find it. The four had seen this arrangement before; they had practically built it by hand. Pavel Kresin admired the screen's confidence. Milan Sarek admired its speed. Vera Dolin, retired and still consulted, said nothing in the meeting and afterwards showed Nadia Orlov a drawer at the railway workshop, where she taught now, set aside for the paper sheets the screen could not hold. It was a sensible arrangement. It was also a private one. Nadia had been asked to write the material for the operations staff who would read the board, and its section on limitations was still blank.
texts.fractured: The new readiness board showed each aircraft as a green or red square, and Nadia Orlov had been asked to write the material for the operations staff who would read it. On the second morning a younger crew chief brought her an envelope of comments. They were in Vera Dolin's square handwriting and asked one question several ways: where did the qualification go when the square turned green? The crew chief carried Nadia's old green marker in his top pocket, its cap worn smooth; she had given it to him years ago, and he had never thought it strange to keep. Vera had not signed the comments. She had not needed to. Nadia read them twice, unsure whether they were addressed to the engineers or to her.

contexts.text: Estovakia was already at war with Emmeria, months before any ministry calendar had expected it. Air units moved west, readiness reports went up the chain twice a day, and every new system was judged by how quickly it could say yes. A board that hesitated was a board somebody would be asked to explain.

Estovakia's civil war was still running. The air arm served one side of a divided country, fields changed hands or loyalties without warning, and a readiness report could cost someone a post if it said the wrong thing to the wrong office. New equipment arrived irregularly; new instructions arrived constantly.

The civil war had ended in a negotiated settlement, and the federation that signed it was trying to look like a state that kept honest books. New systems were part of that effort. Ministries wanted readiness figures they could publish, and for once nobody was sure whether a written qualification would count against a unit or for it.

chapters.default_context: Estovakia entered the spring of 2015 still marked by its long internal war, with a government promising order and armed forces receiving equipment faster than they could learn to use it. Readiness had become a word ministers used in speeches. Nobody outside the hangars asked what it meant on any particular morning.

options.label: Hold my signature until the board can carry a note.
options.reply: The installation slips by a month. The engineers add a narrow qualification field and complain, accurately, that it will slow every morning.

options.label: Sign, and teach the staff to open the attachments.
options.reply: The board goes live on schedule. Whether the operations staff open the attachments will depend on who is teaching them that week.

chapters.title: A Timetable That Needs Pauses

texts.trusted: The letter from the railway's planning office offered Nadia Orlov a desk, a salary and a timetable section that needed someone who understood pauses. She read it in the hangar door, where she could hear wagons coupling on the siding. Vera Dolin admitted at once that she had given them Nadia's name; the railway workshop where she taught apprentices shared a canteen with the planners. Pavel Kresin called it a terrible idea and then, a minute later, probably a good one. Milan Sarek wanted to know who would teach the operations course. Nobody pretended that question was small. Nadia folded the letter along its creases and recognized, in her own hesitation, the serious answer she had once begun in a canteen and made smaller.
texts.compromised: The railway's planning office wrote to offer Nadia Orlov a timetable section that needed someone who understood pauses. She read the letter in the hangar door, with wagons coupling on the siding, and put it in her pocket before anyone could see it. Pavel Kresin saw it anyway. Vera Dolin, who taught apprentices at the railway workshop, looked unsurprised in a way that suggested she had supplied the name and meant never to mention it. Milan Sarek began talking about the operations course as though it could not run without Nadia, which was flattering and untrue. The four had grown skilled at keeping one another. Nadia could feel that warmth closing around the letter, and how easily it would let her decide nothing.
texts.fractured: The railway's planning office wrote to offer Nadia Orlov a timetable section that needed someone who understood pauses. The letter said she had been recommended by a senior instructor at the railway workshop. Only one person there knew how Nadia listened to wagons. Vera Dolin had not written to her in years, and had not written now; she had simply put Nadia's name where it might be useful, and left it there. Nadia read the letter in the hangar door. The younger crew chief, passing with the green marker in his pocket, asked whether it was bad news. She said she did not know yet. It was the first time in years she had not known what she wanted, and she had nobody nearby to ask.

contexts.text: Estovakian forces held Gracemeria. The government called it a decisive success and asked the railways to carry the war west on timetables nobody published. Families learned to read the length of a silence from the front. In the hangars, every square that turned green on a board was an aircraft somebody would be asked to send.

Estovakia had declared war on Emmeria at summer's end and sent its forces across the border. State broadcasts spoke of security and old grievances. Military trains ran at night, readiness reports were wanted twice a day, and people with doubts kept them for kitchens and canteens, where a careless sentence still cost less.

The end of August passed without the declaration the planners had prepared. Estovakia's government withheld the invasion, citing its record of contact with Emmeria and the cost of the civil war years. Officers who had expected orders received exercise schedules instead. Some were relieved, some were angry, and most did not say which in public.

The negotiated federation spent the summer rebuilding ministries rather than armies. Railways carried timber, grain and returning families instead of military trains, and the planning offices that ran them were hiring. For the first time in years, a civilian career for an experienced officer did not look like desertion. It merely looked like a choice.

The civil war still divided Estovakia that autumn. Railways ran when the lines were held and stopped when they were not, and the planners who kept them moving were valued by every side. Air units were short of everything except requests. Leaving the service was possible, but nobody pretended that a departure would be read as neutral.

chapters.default_context: Autumn brought speeches about Estovakia's place on the continent and quieter talk about what those speeches were preparing. Exercises were extended, and the railways were asked for timetables that could change at short notice. Ordinary life went on around the rumours, as it does, with people taking new jobs and turning down others.

options.label: Say aloud that the offer tempts me.
options.reply: Nadia admits the railway tempts her. Nobody laughs, and the operations course must now be planned without assuming she will always run it.

options.label: Keep the letter folded until I am sure.
options.reply: The letter stays in Nadia's pocket, softening at the creases, while the course carries on as though nothing had arrived.

chapters.title: The Jar in the Canteen

texts.trusted: In the canteen Nadia Orlov found one of Pavel Kresin's trainees trying to open a jar against his knee, left-handed. His right shoulder sat a fraction too high. She knew the posture; she had watched it for a whole spring once. Pavel came in, saw the jar and stopped smiling. He said the boy was the best in the class and would heal faster flying than sitting. Then he heard himself, and sat down. Vera Dolin, collecting lunch between classes, said the harness logs would show which side he had been favouring. Milan Sarek had already pencilled the trainee onto next week's roster. Someone switched on the radio. It played the old song, and for once nobody sang.
texts.compromised: One of Pavel Kresin's trainees was trying to open a jar against his knee when Nadia Orlov came into the canteen. His right shoulder sat a fraction too high. Pavel saw her notice. He said quietly that the boy would be fine; he would find him useful work on the ground for a week, and nobody need make a medical case of it. Milan Sarek said the roster could absorb a week. Vera Dolin said she would note the harness adjustment on a sheet in her drawer, where she noted most things the screen would not hold. Every offer was kind. Nadia recognized the whole arrangement: four people catching a young man before he fell, and making sure nobody saw him trip.
texts.fractured: Nadia Orlov found a trainee pilot in the canteen trying to open a jar against his knee with his left hand. His right shoulder sat a fraction too high, and he smiled too quickly when he saw her. She had seen that smile before, on someone who once flew beside her and believed that being useful meant hiding what hurt. That person had taught this class for a while. The habit had outlasted the friendship. The trainee said he could do whatever was needed. Nadia had heard that sentence so often, in another voice, that it almost sounded like an answer. Outside, a van from the railway workshop was delivering the trainees' repaired harnesses, each tagged in a square, familiar hand.

contexts.text: Estovakia had capitulated. Orders now passed through the hands of those who had defeated it, its air units flew only what inspectors permitted, and instructors were told to keep training without being told what for. Canteens were full of young people with too little to fly and a great deal to be anxious about.

Gracemeria had been in Estovakian hands since the autumn. Holding it required aircraft, crews and fuel the training schedules had never planned for, and instructors were pressed to pass students faster. Injuries that would once have meant a month on the ground were now discussed as matters of attitude. Nobody wrote that down.

The war with Emmeria was entering its first winter. Training classes were shortened, students were posted west in the week they qualified, and every squadron competed to report full strength. In that climate a young pilot who admitted pain risked being thought unwilling. Instructors knew it, and did not all agree on what to do.

The withheld invasion had left Estovakia's forces in a strange posture: mobilised, and with nowhere to go. Training continued at wartime pace because nobody had ordered it to slow. Students competed for postings that might never become real, and some hid injuries to stay in a race whose finish line had been quietly removed.

The new federation was shrinking its air arm, and every training class knew that fewer graduates would be kept than had enrolled. Students competed fiercely for the places that remained, and some hid injuries to stay in the running. Instructors who had once complained of shortages now complained of a different scarcity: futures.

The civil war showed no sign of ending before winter. Training units on every side produced pilots as fast as the aircraft allowed, and the aircraft allowed less each month. A trainee who reported an injury could lose his place, and in a divided country a place was also a kind of protection.

chapters.default_context: The first frosts arrived with no war declared and no assurance that one would not be. Training classes continued at an urgent pace for reasons the ministry described only as readiness. Young pilots competed for places and postings, and in that competition a sore shoulder could look like a weakness rather than a fact.

options.label: Ask what hurts before talking about the roster.
options.reply: The trainee tells Nadia which movement he has been avoiding. He loses a month on the roster and keeps his shoulder.

options.label: Find the trainee useful work on the ground.
options.reply: The trainee brightens at being useful. Nadia watches him favour the shoulder all afternoon and decides, for now, to say nothing.

callback.text: The readiness board now carries a narrow qualification field, added after Nadia held her signature. The young operations staff have started to fill it in.

chapters.title: Units, Not Places

texts.trusted: The guard brought the woman into the canteen because the gate was no place to wait in February. She wanted to know where her son's class had been sent. Its postings had gone out at the end of January, naming units rather than places. Pavel Kresin had taught the boy and began telling her what a good pilot he was, then stopped, hearing how little that answered. Milan Sarek offered his own telephone number, as he once would have, and caught Vera Dolin's look. Vera said there was a welfare office whose job this was, and that it was slow. All three were right. The woman held her cup without drinking. Nadia Orlov sat down opposite her and tried to find exactly where her knowledge ended.
texts.compromised: The guard let the woman wait in the canteen, out of the February cold. Her son's class had received its postings at the end of January, units named and places not, and she wanted to know where he was. Milan Sarek murmured that he could find out; he still knew the clerks who knew. Pavel Kresin, who had taught the boy, offered to write to him privately. Vera Dolin kept quiet, which was how she disagreed now. The four could give this woman an answer by evening through doors that were not meant to open. They had done it before, for people they liked. Nadia Orlov watched the cup cool in the woman's hands and wondered what they had done for the people they had never met.
texts.fractured: The guard brought the woman into the canteen out of the February cold. Her son's class had received its postings at the end of January, naming units rather than places, and she wanted to know where he had gone. She said an old instructor at the railway workshop, where the boy had once been an apprentice, had told her to ask for Nadia Orlov by name. 'She said you would tell me what you knew, and stop there.' Nadia understood that Vera Dolin had sent her. It was the nearest thing to a message the two of them had exchanged in years, and it came in the shape of a frightened stranger who needed the truth more than either of them needed forgiving.

contexts.text: Estovakia had capitulated, and its forces abroad were coming home under terms written by others, or were not yet coming home. Families waited at gates across the country for lists that arrived late and incomplete. Whoever answered a parent's question at a gate was, for that moment, the whole of the state.

The fighting with Emmeria had already stopped. Units were recalled, reorganised and counted, and every family with someone in uniform wanted to know when that person would be home. The ministries issued lists and corrected them. In the gaps between corrections, people came to the gate of the nearest base and asked whoever was there.

Estovakian forces still held Gracemeria through the winter, and new graduates were posted west to hold it with them. Families were told the names of units, not cities. Letters were slow and closely read. Parents who had been proud of a son's wings now came to base gates asking whether anyone could say where those wings had taken him.

The war with Emmeria had settled into a hard winter. Graduates were posted as soon as they qualified, families were told little, and state broadcasts spoke of resolve. At base gates across Estovakia the same scene repeated itself: a parent with a photograph, a guard with no authority to answer, and a canteen where someone might.

Estovakia's forces had spent the winter mobilised for an invasion that never came. Graduates were dispersed to fields across the country so that nothing looked like a gathering, and their postings were kept quiet out of habit. Families who had braced for war found themselves unable to learn something as simple as where their child slept.

The negotiated federation was reorganising its air arm field by field. Graduates were posted to bases that had changed names twice, and the personnel offices that tracked them were still being staffed. Families found the confusion maddening rather than frightening. It still brought them to base gates, asking for someone who could read the orders.

The civil war had divided families as well as airfields. A son posted to a unit might be a day's journey away or on a front line, and the orders did not say which. Parents came to whichever base was nearest and hoped the people inside were the right people. Sometimes they were.

chapters.default_context: The winter passed under a cloud of readiness that never quite became rain. Graduates were posted quickly and quietly, and their families were told only the names of units. Rumour filled the space where places should have been. At base gates, parents asked guards questions that guards were not allowed to answer, and were sent inside to wait.

options.label: Tell her exactly what I know, and where it ends.
options.reply: Nadia gives the mother the unit, the date and the edges of her knowledge. It comforts less than a promise, and it will still be true next week.

options.label: Promise her I will find out more.
options.reply: The mother leaves with a promise and a telephone number. Nadia spends the next week learning how much of that promise she can keep.

callback.text: Since Nadia admitted that the railway tempted her, people have told her more about their own wishes. She has learned to listen without promising anything.

chapters.title: What the Drawer Holds

texts.trusted: The request asked for every readiness record from the winter, summaries and detail alike. The four gathered at Vera Dolin's bench in the railway workshop to sort them. Milan Sarek wanted to send the summaries first, because they were complete and would actually be read. Vera laid out the detail sheets with every qualification beside its aircraft and every name beside its qualification. Some of the names were trainees'. Pavel Kresin asked whether a nineteen-year-old who had written 'serviceable for the listed task' at three in the morning deserved to hear that line read aloud in an office. Nadia Orlov thought of how long it had taken her to want her own name beside a limit. They disagreed openly, which was its own kind of progress.
texts.compromised: The request asked for every readiness record from the winter. The summaries were ready; they had always been ready. The rest was in Vera Dolin's drawer at the railway workshop: the improvised repairs, the qualifications the screen could not hold, the sheets the four had kept so that nobody would suffer a public correction. Vera opened the drawer and took nothing out. Milan Sarek said the summaries were accurate as far as they went. Pavel Kresin said some of the names in the drawer belonged to trainees who had done their best at three in the morning. Both were true. Nadia Orlov looked at the drawer and understood that it had been kept for good reasons for so long that the reasons had become the drawer.
texts.fractured: The request asked for every readiness record from the winter, and Nadia Orlov found that the detailed sheets were not where the screen said they would be. The younger crew chief told her, uncomfortably, that the maintenance qualifications had been kept on paper at the railway workshop, because the old chief there had never trusted the board. Nadia went herself. Vera Dolin was at her bench with apprentices around her. For a moment neither spoke. Then Vera opened a drawer, took out a folder thick with handwriting and set it between them. 'Everything,' she said. 'Names too. You decide what goes.' It was the first sentence Vera had spoken to her in years. It was an instruction, and it was trust.

contexts.text: Estovakia had capitulated. Inspectors appointed under the terms of surrender were requesting records from every unit: readiness, maintenance, orders received and orders given. Officially, nothing was burned. Those who had written honest qualifications during the war found that their paperwork had become evidence, and nobody could yet say for whom.

A ceasefire with Emmeria had been signed. Estovakia's forces were standing down from positions they had held through the winter, and the government wanted to know what had been ordered, by whom and on what assurances. Every readiness report from the war had become a document that someone might soon read aloud.

Emmeria had capitulated, and Estovakia's government called the war won. Victory brought its own audits. The ministries wanted readiness records that showed how efficiently the campaign had been fought, and units competed to submit the cleanest accounts. Anyone who had written down a limit during the war now had to decide whether it belonged in a history of success.

The fighting with Emmeria had stopped without a signed ceasefire. The front settled where exhaustion left it, and the ministries began counting what remained. Requests for records came from offices that had not existed a month earlier. Nobody knew which version of the war would become the official one, and everyone suspected the paperwork would decide.

An antigovernment coup had overturned the leadership that planned the invasion of Emmeria, and Estovakia's forces could no longer fight on. The new authorities promised accountability and requested records from every unit. In hangars across the country people reread what they had signed during the winter, wondering whether honesty would now be rewarded, punished or merely filed.

Emmerian forces had retaken Gracemeria, and Estovakian units were falling back east. State broadcasts spoke of regrouping. In the ministries, officials began requesting the winter's readiness records, and it was plain they were looking for someone to hold responsible for the assurances that had been given. The question was whose signatures would be read first.

Gracemeria remained in Estovakian hands into the spring, and the war went on without the quick end that had been promised. The ministries demanded readiness records to prove the campaign could be sustained. Units that reported honest limits were accused of pessimism; units that did not were asked to fly more. Both kinds of report were being kept.

The war with Emmeria continued into spring. Estovakia's government demanded more sorties and better figures, and audits of the winter's readiness records began in earnest. Every unit knew the auditors wanted proof that more was possible. A record showing why it was not could protect a crew, or end a career.

A year without the invasion had turned Estovakia's mobilisation into a budget problem. Auditors wanted to know what the forces had been ready for and what that readiness had cost. Records showing honest limits were suddenly useful arguments for sending people home. Records that hid them argued for something nobody wanted to name.

The negotiated federation was auditing everything, partly to show its own citizens that it could. Readiness records were requested from every unit, with maintenance logs and training reports. For once the auditors seemed to want the truth more than good figures, which made anyone who had kept two sets of records unusually nervous.

The civil war had entered another spring. Each side audited its own units, looking for disloyalty as often as for faults. Readiness records were evidence of capability and also of allegiance. People who had kept honest qualifications wondered whether that honesty would be read as courage, as sabotage, or simply as the work of a careful hand.

chapters.default_context: Spring brought an audit. The ministry wanted every unit's readiness records, maintenance logs and training reports, and it wanted them complete. Nobody said what the audit was for; some thought it was preparation and others thought it was housekeeping. Either way, everyone who had kept two versions of the truth had to decide which one to send.

options.label: Send the detail with every name left in.
options.reply: The record arrives whole. Some names in it belong to people who will face hard questions, and Nadia's is the first of them.

options.label: Send the summaries; keep the detail ready.
options.reply: The office receives a clean account. The detail waits for someone who asks precisely enough to be given it.

callback.text: The trainee who admitted his shoulder in the canteen has his full movement back. His harness log still shows the month on the ground, and nobody has tidied it away.

chapters.title: A Question Instead of a Rule

texts.trusted: Nadia Orlov's last operations course before the railway took her ended at Vera Dolin's bench, because Vera said trainees ought to see where qualifications were born. Vera stood at the bench pretending not to teach. Milan Sarek had brought his brother, visiting for once, who wanted to see what Milan actually did and was faintly disappointed by how many forms it involved. Pavel Kresin sang the old song under his breath as he stacked stools, using the words he preferred. A trainee asked Nadia for one rule to carry when a request outran the aircraft. Nadia took a green marker from the bench and uncapped it. The four had argued over that rule for twenty-five years. She thought the trainees deserved the argument.
texts.compromised: Nadia Orlov brought her operations trainees to the railway workshop for their last session, because Vera Dolin had offered the bench and because the drawer was there. Nobody mentioned the drawer. Pavel Kresin showed the trainees how a clean summary was assembled, and did it well. Milan Sarek explained how a familiar voice could make a request sound settled. Vera said little. A trainee, comparing a summary with the bench log, asked why a qualification was missing from one and present in the other. The room went quiet in a way all four recognized. Pavel reached for the clean sheet and stopped. The trainee was waiting for a rule. Ten years earlier another had asked almost the same question, and the old crew had been deciding its answer ever since.
texts.fractured: Nadia Orlov's operations course ended the year with a visit to the railway workshop, arranged by the younger crew chief. Vera Dolin met the trainees at the door, showed them the bench and the drawer of qualification sheets, and then went to teach in the next room, leaving Nadia's class to Nadia. It was a courtesy, and they both knew it. The crew chief took the old green marker from his pocket and asked Nadia, in front of her trainees, the question she had asked him when she gave it away: what would she write beside an offer she could honestly keep? The trainees waited for her answer. Through the wall Nadia could hear Vera's voice correcting someone, patiently.

contexts.text: Estovakia ended 2016 a defeated country. Its air arm had been reduced under the terms of capitulation, its training schools were permitted to teach maintenance and air traffic but little else, and many experienced officers were leaving for civilian work. Some went bitterly. Others went as though they had only been waiting for permission.

The ceasefire with Emmeria had held through the summer and into autumn. Estovakia's forces were home or coming home, questions about the war's planning were being asked in the capital, and the air arm was shrinking to a size a peacetime budget could keep. Instructors taught smaller classes, and several were asked, quietly, what they had signed in 2015.

Estovakia ended the year as the victor of a war it was still paying for. Its forces remained across the border, state broadcasts celebrated, and the air arm was told to keep its wartime pace without its wartime budget. Instructors who had taught limits throughout the war found that victory had not made those limits any less real.

The war with Emmeria had ended without a signed ceasefire, in a silence the two governments described differently. Estovakia's air arm was reorganised twice in a year, and many officers took civilian posts, some by choice. Newspapers began, cautiously, to print letters asking what the war had been for and who had promised it would be quick.

Estovakia had refused the ceasefire after the coup and fought on, and the war was dragging toward a second winter nobody had planned for. Training schools ran without enough aircraft or instructors. Officers who asked to leave were refused or quietly let go, depending on whom they asked. Everyone was tired in the same way.

contexts.text: Estovakian forces still held Gracemeria as the second winter of the war approached. The occupation had become routine without becoming settled. Classes graduated into it, families wrote letters into it, and the ministries reported it as success. Instructors were asked to teach more pilots in less time and to call that efficiency.

The war with Emmeria was still unresolved as 2016 ended. Training schools operated at wartime pace without wartime supplies, and experienced officers were stretched across more classes than any honest timetable could contain. Some asked for transfers to the railways or the ports, where the work was also hard but at least had a destination.

Estovakia ended 2016 having withheld its invasion and kept the peace for more than a year. The mobilisation was being slowly unwound, and officers who had prepared for a war that did not come were offered posts in the railways, ministries and ports. The country had not resolved its grievances; it had chosen, for now, not to settle them by force.

The negotiated federation finished its second year with its borders quiet and its budgets argued over in public. The air arm was smaller and better documented than it had ever been. Experienced officers moved freely into civilian work, and the training schools had begun to sound less like barracks and more like colleges.

Estovakia's civil war entered another winter. Each side trained its own pilots, kept its own records and told its own story. Railways, workshops and airfields changed hands or allegiances. Experienced people did what they could inside whichever institution still functioned near them, and hoped the work would outlast the faction that paid for it.

chapters.default_context: The year ended without a war on Estovakia's western border and without certainty that there would never be one. The air arm trimmed its classes, the railways hired, and the ministries spoke of a new stability. People who had spent their careers preparing for the worst began, carefully, to prepare for something else.

options.label: Give them the question instead of a rule.
options.reply: The trainees leave with something harder to remember and easier to use. Within a week Nadia hears it repeated, slightly wrong and entirely useful.

options.label: Give them a rule short enough to carry.
options.reply: The rule is clear and portable. Its exceptions will have to be learned the way Nadia learned them, from the people who bear the cost.

callback.text: The mother from the canteen has written to Nadia. Her son's letters reach home again, and she thanks Nadia for telling her only what was true.
